implementation_notes: Java's profiling story is strong (async-profiler for the CPU and allocation flame graphs, JFR for a production-safe recording, Eclipse MAT for heap analysis) and the micro-optimisations that pay at a measured hotspot are mostly allocation and dispatch: eliminating boxing in hot generics, replacing a megamorphic call site, avoiding the allocation of a lambda or an iterator in a loop, and improving data layout (primitive arrays over object arrays). Java's specific trap is that a micro-benchmark measures the wrong tier of the JIT - a method runs interpreted, then C1, then C2 - so a short JMH benchmark without warm-up measures the interpreter, and the JIT is measuring itself; JMH's warm-up and fork model exist for exactly this. Escape analysis is the other Java-specific tool: if it succeeds, an allocation disappears entirely, which is why -XX:+PrintEscapeAnalysis and a flat layout matter.
idiom_name: async-profiler / JFR attribution plus JMH with warm-up iterations and forks, applied at the measured hotspot
pitfalls: Benchmarking without warm-up: the method runs interpreted then C1 then C2, so a short JMH run without @Warmup measures the interpreter.
A megamorphic call site (three or more receiver types) is never inlined by the JIT, and no source-level hint fixes it - make the site monomorphic.
Boxing in a hot generic (Integer in a List<Integer>) allocates and adds a pointer chase; use a primitive-specialised collection or an array.
A lambda or stream pipeline per loop iteration allocates; the allocation profile shows it where the CPU profile just shows a low-level call.
async-profiler with default settings may show the wrong thing; for memory use the alloc profile, not the CPU profile.
